prompt.context: Our client is a manufacturer of ball bearings. The company has had flat sales and declining profits for the last 3 years. The CEO believes that high-margin service businesses built on existing core competencies are the answer to his problem.
prompt.question: From a Value Chain perspective, how would you assess whether or not there are opportunities to build sustainable new service businesses? Develop some potential business models based on your assessment.

clarifying_info.q: What are the company's key strengths or core competencies?
clarifying_info.a: The company has a world-class procurement department with strong processes and personnel. It also has access to 2,000 buyers that work for its parent company.

clarifying_info.q: Who are the company's major customers?
clarifying_info.a: The company has strong customer relationships with large manufacturing companies such as Caterpillar and John Deere.

clarifying_info.q: How do the major customers currently manage their supply base?
clarifying_info.a: Large manufacturing companies typically buy several hundred components from around 500 suppliers, but build strategic relationships including electronic linkages with only their top 20 suppliers.

framework: Map the full value chain: procurement, inbound logistics, manufacturing/operations, outbound logistics, sales & marketing, service
Identify core competencies at each step — where does the client have world-class capabilities vs. parity?
Assess which competencies could be monetized as a service for external customers
Screen potential service business models on: sustainability of competitive advantage, market size, customer willingness to pay, fit with existing assets
Develop and stress-test selected business models

questions.prompt: Walk through the value chain and identify where the client has a core competency that could become the basis of a new service business.
questions.guidance: Strong candidates should quickly identify procurement as the standout core competency: world-class processes, skilled personnel, and access to 2,000 parent-company buyers. They should note that the client also has deep customer relationships with large OEMs (Caterpillar, John Deere), which provides a route to market for new services.

questions.prompt: Major manufacturing customers manage strategic supplier relationships electronically with their top 20 suppliers, but have ~500 suppliers total. What business opportunity does this gap create?
questions.guidance: Candidates should identify that beyond the top 20 suppliers, extending electronic/strategic linkages is not cost-effective for the customer to do themselves — yet significant cost savings could still be unlocked there. The client's procurement competency and existing electronic linkages position it to manage those sub-top-20 suppliers on behalf of its major customers, capturing value through a managed-services or outsourced-procurement model.

questions.prompt: Describe the specific business model you would recommend and explain why it is sustainable.
questions.guidance: Recommended model: the client acts as an outsourced procurement manager for the non-strategic (below-top-20) suppliers of its major manufacturing customers. It leverages its web-enabled electronic linkages to reduce costs and streamline procurement for those components. Sustainability drivers: (1) proprietary electronic infrastructure is hard to replicate; (2) deep customer trust/relationships create switching costs; (3) parent-company buyer network provides scale advantage; (4) compounding data/process advantages over time.

brainstorming.prompt: What other service business models could the client explore beyond the recommended procurement-outsourcing model?

categories.name: Procurement & Supply Chain Services
ideas: Outsourced supplier management for sub-top-20 suppliers of OEM customers
Group purchasing / aggregated buying on behalf of multiple OEM customers
Supply chain risk monitoring and analytics

categories.name: Information & Data Services
ideas: Market intelligence on component pricing and supplier performance
Electronic catalog and e-procurement platform licensing
Benchmarking reports for component costs across industries

categories.name: Logistics & Distribution Services
ideas: Consolidated inbound logistics management for OEM customers
Just-in-time delivery coordination for non-critical components

categories.name: Consulting & Advisory
ideas: Procurement process improvement consulting for mid-size manufacturers
Digital transformation advisory for supply chain

categories.name: Financial Services
ideas: Supply chain financing / early payment programs for suppliers
Insurance products for supply chain disruption

recommendation: Recommend building a new outsourced procurement service business targeting the client's existing OEM customers (Caterpillar, John Deere, etc.)

The service will manage suppliers that fall outside each customer's top-20 strategic suppliers, leveraging the client's world-class procurement processes, personnel, and existing web-enabled electronic linkages to reduce costs and streamline the procurement process for those components
risks: Channel conflict if OEM customers perceive the client is overstepping its supplier role
Difficulty pricing the service and demonstrating ROI to procurement executives
Execution risk in scaling the procurement team to handle multiple customers' sub-top-20 supplier bases
Dependence on parent-company buyer network — risk if parent relationship changes
next_steps: Pilot with one anchor OEM customer to prove the cost savings case and refine the service model
Define the pricing model (fee-for-service, gain-sharing, or subscription)
Build or adapt the electronic linkage platform to support multi-customer managed procurement
Assess talent requirements and whether parent-company buyers can be leveraged contractually
Develop a roadmap from planning phase to full commercialization
